Directionality boundary: the strongest cohort evidence on this pair runs from depression to burning mouth syndrome (upstream), not from this primary; this edge documents only the comorbidity association and must never be presented as depression caused by burning mouth syndrome.
governanceNotes: Authored as ASSOCIATION_ONLY with NOT_ESTABLISHED consensus: a 1:4 propensity-matched nationwide cohort reports roughly 3.4-fold higher adjusted hazard of incident burning mouth syndrome among patients with depression (and roughly 5.1-fold for anxiety), clinical reviews consistently rank depression and anxiety among the most frequent associated conditions, and the pain is understood as a chronic neuropathic orofacial pain disorder; but the dominant measured direction is the upstream one and the literature explicitly frames psychological factors as contributors the diagnosis must exclude, so the edge documents comorbidity only.

Conservatism boundaries: the cohort cannot establish which condition came first in any pair, case definitions vary across studies, reviews warn against invoking psychiatric causation without thorough evaluation, and BMS by definition has no identifiable organic cause at diagnosis, making any unidirectional mood-consequence claim unfounded at the mapping level.

Duplicate-scope check: no edges exist from this primary or into depressive-disorder from another orofacial-pain identity in the registry; the trigeminal-neuralgia -> depressive-disorder edge belongs to a different primary with its own evidence base and is not duplicate scope.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: A nationwide propensity-matched cohort (1:4 matching, survival analysis) reports an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.37 (95 percent CI 1.67-6.80) for incident burning mouth syndrome among patients with depression and 5.09 (95 percent CI 2.19-11.80) for anxiety, with female sex carrying higher risk, while dermatology and orofacial-pain reviews consistently list depression, anxiety, and cancerphobia among the most frequently associated conditions in BMS populations; the evidence base is explicitly bidirectional or reverse-directed, since the cohort measured mood disorders as the upstream exposure.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the strongest cohort evidence runs from depression to burning mouth syndrome (the reverse of this edge's direction), cross-sectional psychiatric comorbidity in pain populations cannot establish direction, chronic orofacial pain and mood disorders share neurotransmitter and stress-axis pathways that could produce the association in either direction, and a depressive disorder can only be attributed as a consequence of the pain after excluding preexisting mood disorder and the sensory, endocrine, nutritional, and medication causes that the BMS diagnostic algorithm itself requires ruling out, so no directional claim is made here.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized chronic-neuropathic-pain comorbidity pathway has been described: burning mouth syndrome is characterized as a chronic neuropathic orofacial pain disorder, and chronic pain states share central monoamine dysregulation, stress-axis activation, sleep disruption, and functional-disability pathways with depressive disorders, which would explain the documented co-occurrence; the mood-to-pain direction is equally plausible under the same shared pathways (the cohort's upstream finding), and reviews emphasize that psychological factors may contribute to symptom intensity without being the cause, so the coupling explains the comorbidity without establishing that burning mouth syndrome caused a depressive disorder in any individual, and preexisting mood disorder, medication effects, and shared neurotransmitter substrate remain active competing explanations, so no directional claim is made here.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Burning mouth syndrome and depressive disorders co-occur at multiples of background rates in cohort and review data, but the measured direction is predominantly reverse, so individual determination requires documented BMS against accepted criteria (normal mucosa, exclusion of organic causes) with chronology, psychiatric diagnosis of a depressive disorder against accepted criteria at a defined time point, mood and pain documentation at relevant time points, and exclusion of preexisting mood disorder and medication effects, all reviewed case by case by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documented burning mouth syndrome against accepted criteria (chronic oral burning with normal clinical mucosal examination and exclusion of organic causes) with onset chronology; psychiatric assessment establishing a depressive disorder against accepted criteria with temporality relative to the oral pain; mood-measure and pain-intensity documentation at relevant time points; medication and substance review including antidepressant and anxiolytic effects; competing-explanation review including preexisting mood disorder, xerostomia, nutritional deficiency, candidiasis, and endocrine contributors; a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Preexisting or independent major depressive disorder unrelated to the oral pain
Medication effects on mood related to treatment of the oral pain or comorbid conditions
Dry mouth, nutritional deficiency, candidiasis, or endocrine dysfunction as both pain driver and mood contributor
Anxiety or cancerphobia syndromes masquerading as or amplifying the pain-mood association

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the comorbidity is documented in cohort and review literature, but the measured direction is predominantly depression-to-BMS, the reviews warn against invoking psychiatric causation without thorough evaluation, and chronic-pain mood comorbidity is bidirectional by nature, so this edge flags the comorbidity for evidence-gap review only and must never be presented as established causation or aggravation.

sourceReferences.citation: Lee SJ, Kim C, Yu H, Kim DK. Relationship of Depression, Anxiety, and Bipolar Disease with Burning Mouth Syndrome: A Nationwide Cohort Study. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023;20(4):3391. PMID 36834086. doi:10.3390/ijerph20043391.
sourceReferences.note: Nationwide 1:4 propensity-matched cohort reporting adjusted hazard ratios of 3.37 (depression) and 5.09 (anxiety) for incident burning mouth syndrome, with bipolar disorder showing no significant risk; the abstract frames mood disorders as the upstream exposure, which is why this edge records the direction as reverse-dominant and stays at association strength.

sourceReferences.note: Clinical review listing depression, anxiety, and cancerphobia as the most frequently associated conditions in burning mouth syndrome populations while warning that psychiatric causes should not be invoked without thorough evaluation and that multiple contributing factors are common; anchors the comorbidity proposition and the exclusion discipline the diagnostic algorithm requires.
